kurz: Why, unlike with a lump-sum investment, the order of returns determines the outcome when you withdraw money, and why the well-known withdrawal rules from American studies do not take German taxation into account.

bloecke.md: An investor who invests a sum once and neither pays in nor withdraws anything for 30 years reaches the same final value regardless of whether the bad years came at the beginning or at the end, because the order does not matter when the annual returns are multiplied. As soon as money is withdrawn, this no longer applies. When money is withdrawn in a loss year, units are sold at a low price, and these units are permanently missing in the recovery. Almost everything that distinguishes a withdrawal strategy from a savings plan follows from this difference. It is also the reason why there is no simple answer to the question “how much can I take out each year”.

## Origin of the 4% rule

In 1994, in the *Journal of Financial Planning*, William Bengen examined which real withdrawal a US portfolio of shares and bonds would have sustained for 30 years in any starting year since 1926. He arrived at around 4% of the starting assets in the first year. This amount is then increased each year in line with [[inflation]], regardless of how the portfolio performs. The so-called Trinity study by Cooley, Hubbard and Walz (1998) re-examined the same question in terms of a probability of success for different equity allocations and withdrawal periods. Its tables have been cited ever since.

Both studies are methodologically sound. In everyday use, however, their results are often misrepresented.

- The 4% figure does not refer to the current portfolio value at any given time. The percentage is applied only once, in the first year. After that, the withdrawal is a fixed amount in euros adjusted for inflation, which no longer depends on the portfolio value. With starting assets of €500,000, that is €20,000, even if the portfolio falls to 300,000.
- The rule does not guarantee success; it states a success rate. In the tables, “success” only meant that more than zero was left after 30 years. Even a portfolio in which only €4,000 remains after 30 years counts as a success.
- The results apply before costs and before tax. The calculations used index series, without [[Flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)|flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer)]], fund costs or custody fees.
- The rule is based on US data. In the 20th century, American shares and bonds performed better than those in most other developed countries.

For German investors, the last point weighs most heavily. In 2010, Wade Pfau repeated the calculation using the long-term series of Dimson, Marsh and Staunton for 17 countries. In only a few of them, including the USA, Canada and Denmark, would a real withdrawal of 4% historically have lasted for 30 years. Germany, Japan, Italy and France were well below this. In Germany, the hyperinflation of 1923 and the currency reform of 1948 destroyed most nominal wealth twice within 25 years; in 1948, savings balances were converted at a ratio of 100 to 6.5. Bonds, which serve as a buffer in the US calculation, lost most of their value in both cases. Adopting 4% as a universally valid figure means taking the history of a single, exceptionally successful country as the basis.

## Sequence-of-returns risk

[[Sequence-of-returns risk]] can be shown without a simulation. Two portfolios each start with €500,000, and €20,000 is withdrawn from each at the end of every year. Both experience the same five annual returns, only in reverse order: minus 20%, minus 10%, plus 5%, plus 25% and plus 30%. Without withdrawals, both portfolios would reach the same amount of €614,250. With withdrawals, this is not the case.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with €500,000 starting assets and a €20,000 withdrawal at the end of each year; after five years, the two portfolios are €58,918 apart purely because of the order of returns.

bloecke.md: The first five to ten years of retirement largely determine how things develop afterwards. A crash at 65 has a different effect from the same crash at 85. In the first case, 25 more withdrawals have to be paid from the shrunken capital afterwards, in the second only five.

## Withdrawal rules and their trade-offs

Every withdrawal rule weighs two goals against each other: an income that is as stable as possible and the lowest possible probability that the capital is used up before the end of life. The two goals cannot both be maximised at the same time.

bloecke.md: With the fixed real withdrawal, the risk that the capital runs out is greatest. At the same time, it is the only rule that continues to pay out unchanged even when prices fall sharply. With the fixed percentage withdrawal, the capital cannot run out. In return, the withdrawal falls with the market, so after a 40% decline, income also falls by 40%. The rules in the following sections lie between these two approaches.

## The Guyton and Klinger guardrails

In 2006, Jonathan Guyton and William Klinger published a set of rules that changes the fixed withdrawal only when the current [[withdrawal rate]] leaves a corridor around the starting rate. The withdrawal rate is the annual withdrawal divided by the current portfolio value. A corridor of ±20% is usual; with a starting rate of 4%, the guardrails are therefore at 4.8% and 3.2%. Under an additional inflation rule, the inflation adjustment is skipped if the portfolio return in the previous year was negative.

The portfolio starts with €500,000 and a withdrawal of €20,000, that is, 4.0%. The guardrails are at 4.8% and 3.2%.

First, the portfolio slumps to €350,000.

1. Because of the negative year, the inflation rule means there is no increase; the withdrawal stays at €20,000 instead of €20,600.
2. The current rate of 20,000 ÷ 350,000 = 5.71% is above the upper guardrail.
3. The capital preservation rule cuts the withdrawal by 10% to €18,000; the new rate is 5.14%.

The rule cuts only once a year. If the portfolio stays low, the withdrawal is cut again the following year. The adjustment is deliberately sluggish so that a single bad quarter does not trigger a panic decision.

The portfolio then recovers to €620,000.

The rate of 18,000 ÷ 620,000 = 2.90% is now below the lower guardrail. The withdrawal is increased by 10% to €19,800 (3.19%). Two years later, €200 of the €2,000 cut still remains.

A second approach makes the rate depend on market valuation rather than on your own portfolio value. The basic idea is that people who retire when markets are highly valued have worse starting conditions and should therefore withdraw less.

bloecke.erklaerung: The rule derives the withdrawal rate from the CAPE. The reciprocal 1/CAPE is the cyclically adjusted earnings yield of the market. The rate rises when shares are cheap and falls when they are expensive.

bloecke.md: The coefficients a and b are not derived from theory. They were fitted to the same historical series from which the 4% rule also comes. A formula whose parameters were fitted to past data says no more about the future than the past itself. What is robust about the idea is the direction (expensive market, lower rate), less so the exact numerical value.

## Effect of a cash buffer

The most common measure against sequence risk is a buffer covering two to three years of requirements in an [[instant-access savings account]] or a [[money market fund]]. In crash years, withdrawals are taken from this buffer instead of selling shares. The buffer helps, but for a different reason from the one usually given.

Arithmetically, a buffer is an increased cash allocation. A portfolio with 88% shares and 12% in an instant-access savings account that is rebalanced annually behaves practically the same whether or not you call the 12% a “buffer”. With [[rebalancing]], sales are made from the overweight asset class anyway, so after a crash they automatically come from bonds and cash rather than from shares. The benefit of the buffer lies in behavioural economics. A visibly separate account that covers the withdrawals for three years reduces the likelihood of selling shares after all when prices are at their low.

The portfolio amounts to €600,000, and the annual requirement from the portfolio is €24,000. A buffer of three years' requirements amounts to €72,000, that is, 12% of the assets.

If the expected return on the equity portion is four percentage points above the interest rate on instant-access savings, the buffer costs 12% × 4 points = 0.48 percentage points a year on total assets, around €2,880 in the first year. This cost is not zero, but it can be quantified, and it is considerably smaller than the damage caused by a panic sale.

## Partial sale or distribution

The choice between a partial sale and a distribution is mainly about taxes, and the German legal position differs markedly from the Anglo-Saxon focus on dividends. When part of an accumulating fund is sold, only the gain portion of the units sold is taxable (Section 16(1) no. 3 and Section 19 InvStG, Investment Tax Act; Section 20(1) no. 3 EStG, Income Tax Act). The portion corresponding to the capital paid in flows back tax-free. A distribution, by contrast, counts in full as income (Section 16(1) no. 1 InvStG, Section 20(1) no. 3 EStG), even if economically it partly just returns capital.

The assumptions are an equity ETF with a 30% [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]], a [[Saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag)|saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag)]] of €1,000 that is still available and a tax rate of 25% + solidarity surcharge = 26.375%.

Distribution of €15,000: 15,000 × 70% = 10,500 taxable, minus 1,000 = 9,500, of which 26.375% = €2,506 tax.

Partial sale of €15,000 with a 60% gain portion: gain 9,000 × 70% = 6,300, minus 1,000 = 5,300, of which 26.375% = €1,398 tax.

The difference of €1,108 corresponds to just over 7% of the withdrawal and arises every year. The only argument against the partial sale is that it requires a decision. The distribution comes automatically and uses the allowance even if you would not otherwise have sold anything at all.

bloecke.unter: The longer the money was invested, the higher the gain portion of the units sold and thus the tax ratio; even with an 80% gain portion, the tax is only around 14% of the withdrawal and not 26.375%.

bloecke.md: You cannot choose the gain portion freely. Under the [[FIFO]] rule in Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG, the units bought first are deemed to be sold first, and these are the oldest units with the highest gain portion. To control the order, you need several securities accounts, which can also be held at the same bank, and you decide from the outset which one will be closed first.

bloecke.md: The [[Most-favourable assessment (Günstigerprüfung)|most-favourable assessment]] matters more in retirement than during working life. Since July 2026, a standard pension has been around €1,913 gross a month. For pensions starting in 2026, 84% of this is taxable, and the health and long-term care insurance contributions of around 12.35% of the gross pension are deductible as special expenses (Sonderausgaben). Taxable income is therefore often in a tax bracket in which the marginal tax rate is below 25%. In this case, assessment at the personal tax rate is more favourable than the flat-rate withholding tax. The comparison covers the total tax including solidarity surcharge and church tax. The advantage only ends when the tax under the standard scale on the capital income would be higher than the flat-rate withholding tax with its surcharges. The tax office calculates the exact threshold; for single persons with a standard pension, under the 2026 tax scale it is roughly at a taxable income of €30,000 with church tax and €34,000 without.

The base interest rate (Basiszins) for 2026 is 3.20% (BMF circular of 13 January 2026). 70% of this is applied, that is, 2.24% of the fund value at the start of the year. The amount is capped at the fund's increase in value during the year and is reduced by distributions.

With a portfolio value of €600,000, this results in an [[Advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)|advance lump sum]] of €13,440, €9,408 after partial exemption and €8,408 after deducting the €1,000 allowance. At 26.375%, this gives a tax of around €2,218. The bank collects it from the settlement account in January, without a single unit having been sold. If the account is empty, the bank may use an arranged overdraft if the investor has not objected to this in advance. Otherwise, it reports the shortfall to the tax office, and the tax office for the place of residence collects the tax retrospectively in the assessment. The law does not provide for a forced sale of units. A withdrawal plan should therefore be set up so that the settlement account is not empty in December.

bloecke.unter: The routine consists of one appointment in January, one calculation and three possible outcomes; no further control is needed in the withdrawal phase.

bloecke.md:
The classic studies use real historical time series and run through every possible starting year once. This preserves relationships that a random number generator does not capture, such as the reversion of valuations to the mean, the link between inflation and bond yields, and real crash patterns. The disadvantage is the thin data basis. With 100 years of history, there are only just over 70 overlapping 30-year windows, and these overlap so much that they are not independent observations.

A [[Monte Carlo simulation]], by contrast, generates any number of paths from an assumed distribution. This produces smooth probabilities, which, however, reflect exactly the assumptions that were fed into the model. If a normal distribution without autocorrelation is assumed, extreme years are too rare and recovery phases too weak. A success rate of “94%” from a calculator therefore describes a property of the model and not a probability. It is useful as a measure for comparing two rules, not as an absolute statement.

- Choose a starting rate below 4% if the portfolio is global rather than US-heavy and costs and taxes still have to be deducted.
- Set down a rule in writing before the first crash comes. The guardrails only work if they are fixed in advance.
- Cover the expenses you cannot do without (rent, insurance, food) from secure sources, that is, from the statutory pension and, where applicable, an [[immediate annuity]]. Only the remaining part of the expenses should depend on the capital market.
- Schedule the January appointment firmly in order to note the portfolio value, calculate the rate, cover the advance lump sum and check the exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag).

mitnehmen: In the withdrawal phase, the order of returns determines the outcome alongside the average return; in the example, the same five years in reverse order led to a difference of €58,918.
The 4% rule is based on US data before costs and taxes; internationally, only a few markets would have sustained this rate, and historically Germany would not.
Rules with guardrails trade moderate fluctuations in income for greater security of capital; cuts are made only when the current rate leaves the corridor.
For tax purposes, a partial sale is almost always more favourable than a distribution of the same amount, because only the gain portion is taxed.
The tax on the advance lump sum is collected in January regardless of any withdrawal and therefore belongs in the annual plan as a separate item.

begriffe.text: Highest share of the starting assets that could be withdrawn, adjusted for inflation, over a fixed period without the capital being used up before the end of the period in any historical starting year. It is also known as SAFEMAX or the safe withdrawal rate.

Limits set around the initial withdrawal rate, usually ±20%. If the current rate leaves this corridor, the withdrawal is cut or increased by a fixed percentage. The guardrails form the central part of the set of rules by Guyton and Klinger (2006).

Price divided by the inflation-adjusted average earnings of the past ten years, also called CAPE. The ratio smooths out business cycles and serves as a valuation measure from which valuation-based withdrawal rules derive their rate.

The risk of living longer than your own capital lasts. Withdrawal rules can limit it. It can only be handed over completely through a lifelong pension payment, which comes at the expense of being able to leave an inheritance and of flexibility.
